newsitem.title: MEXICO: MEXICO'S FOX ATTACKS PLAN TO CUT VALUE-ADDED TAX.
newsitem.headline: MEXICO'S FOX ATTACKS PLAN TO CUT VALUE-ADDED TAX.

text.p: MEXICO CITY, Aug 6 (Rueter) - An influential member of Mexico's conservative opposition party criticized his party's proposal to cut gradually the country's value-added (IVA) tax to 10 percent from 15 percent.
Guanajuato state governor Vicente Fox told Reuters in an interview late on Tuesday that he thought Mexico needed to raise more tax dollars to fund development and not less.
"If we weaken the government's economic power, who is going to do the state's homework, who will build the roads, the ports, the airports, the hospitals, the schools," he said.

Fox's National Action Party (PAN) has said it will work with other opposition parties to reduce the IVA tax once the lower house of Congress begins its session in September. For the first time this century, Mexican voters handed the opposition a majority during July 6 mid-term polls.
Fox said he thought the proposal would be used by the opposition as a bargaining chip to negotiate wide-ranging tax reform that would improve collection.
"The VAT tax cut will be negotiated in exchange for a real fiscal reform that will take time to work out and will probably not come into effect until 1998," he said.

The tax became an explosive political issue when the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) raised the tax during the worst of Mexico's recent recession so that it could cure sickly public finances.
Fox said Mexico takes in only about 15 percent of GDP in taxes, much lower than the 30 percent or so in the United States and the 40 percent levels of European nations.
He said the problem is a huge informal economy where millions of entrepreneurs do not pay taxes and mistrust of the government that breeds evasion.
"We don't need higher taxes. The problem is the government is inefficient and corrupt. There is no trust in the government so people don't pay taxes," he said.
